mainTopic: Erasures in documents, and forgery worries about witnesses signing on the back
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא about corrections in a document. A word added between the lines can be saved by a note at the end, but an erasure ruins the document. The rule is then limited: an erasure only matters if it sits where 'שריר וקיים' belongs and is big enough to have held those sealing words. Next, the גמרא raises a forgery worry against רב ירמיה בר אבא, who holds that witnesses sign on the back, opposite the writing. The answer is that they sign from bottom to top, running sideways to the lines. A further worry follows: a cheater could cut off the last line together with the first word of a witness's name, and the leftover piece would still count as a valid signature. The גמרא answers that the name is split across lines, and then that the word עד is left out. It then begins a second answer: עד really was written, but we know something definite about this signature. That answer finishes on the next amud.

steps.title: An erasure ruins the document even if it is noted at the end
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by ruling that a document with an erasure is פסול, even if the erasure was noted at the bottom.
steps.simpleTranslation: A document with an erasure is invalid, even if the erasure was confirmed at the end of the document.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its list of corrections by ruling that an erasure ruins the document. Noting it at the end does not help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier in the ברייתא, a word added between the lines can be saved by writing at the end which word was added on which line. An erasure is treated more strictly, and the same note at the end does not save it. The next step explains exactly when this strict rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: An erasure; a spot where writing was scraped off and written over
Invalid
Confirmed; here, noted and approved at the end of the document

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with a word squeezed in between the lines. That kind of correction can be saved by a note at the end, but an erasure cannot.

phrases.english: An erasure: invalid,
even if it is confirmed.
phrases.notes: Confirmed means the correction was written up at the bottom of the document, as in 'on line such-and-such, this word is written.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מְחָק – פָּסוּל, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְּקוּיָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא's list of document corrections that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An erasure makes a document invalid, even when it is noted at the end.

steps.title: The erasure rule only applies where 'שריר וקיים' would go
steps.stepSummary: The rule against erasures is limited. It applies only when the erasure is in the spot for 'שריר וקיים' and is large enough to have held those words.
steps.simpleTranslation: They only said an erasure makes the document invalid when it is in the place of 'שריר וקיים' and is the size of 'שריר וקיים'.
steps.whatsHappening: The text narrows the rule from Step 1 and tells us exactly which erasures ruin a document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'שריר וקיים' (everything is confirmed and established) seal the document. Once they are written, nothing more can be added. The worry is that someone erased these sealing words so that he could add more text. If the erasure is somewhere else, or too small to have held those words, the document stays כשר.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Firm and established', the closing words that seal a document
The size or amount of
'They only said...', a phrase that limits a rule

steps.whatToRemember: Erasures are only a problem when they could hide a forged change to 'שריר וקיים', the words that seal the document.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the strictness about erasures exists only to block one kind of forgery: removing the seal of the document so more can be written.

phrases.english: And they only said an erasure is invalid
in the place of 'confirmed and established',
phrases.notes: These are the closing words of a document. After them, nothing else counts as part of the deal.

phrases.english: and the size of 'confirmed and established'.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא אָמְרוּ מְחָק פָּסוּל אֶלָּא בִּמְקוֹם שָׁרִיר וְקַיָּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the erasure rule from Step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An erasure ruins a document only if it is in the place of 'שריר וקיים' and big enough to have held those words.

steps.title: A forgery worry if witnesses sign on the back
steps.stepSummary: According to רב ירמיה בר אבא, witnesses sign on the back opposite the writing. A worry is raised: someone could add text on the front and then add more witnesses on the back to cover the extra space.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רב ירמיה בר אבא, who says the witnesses sign on the back of the writing, opposite the writing on the outside, we should worry: maybe the holder will write whatever he wants on the inside, then have extra witnesses sign on the outside, and say, 'I did it to add more witnesses.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב ירמיה בר אבא's view of where witnesses sign, because it seems to leave room for forgery.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If witnesses sign on the back to match the length of the writing, a forger could write more lines on the front. He would then add more witness signatures on the back so the signatures still cover all the writing. If anyone asked why there are so many witnesses, he would claim he just wanted extra witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: On the back of the writing
'Let us worry', a phrase that raises a concern
On the inside / on the outside
Extra witnesses

phrases.english: And according to רב ירמיה בר אבא, who says:
behind the writing, opposite the writing, on the outside;

phrases.aramaic: לֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא כָּתֵיב מִגַּוַּאי מַאי דְּבָעֵי,
phrases.english: let us worry: perhaps he will write on the inside whatever he wants,
and have extra witnesses sign on the outside,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר: אֲנָא לְרַבּוֹת בְּעֵדִים הוּא דַּעֲבַדִי!
phrases.english: and say: 'I did it to add more witnesses!'

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא דְּאָמַר אֲחוֹרֵי הַכְּתָב וּכְנֶגֶד הַכְּתָב מִבַּחוּץ לֵיחוּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from erasures to a new forgery worry about where witnesses sign.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ירמיה בר אבא's view that witnesses sign on the back, opposite the writing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Signatures placed to match the text could be extended along with added text, leaving a forgery with a ready excuse.

steps.title: Witnesses sign from bottom to top, so nothing can be added
steps.stepSummary: The answer: the witnesses do not sign one under the other from the top. They sign from bottom to top, running sideways to the lines, so added text would be noticed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Do you think the witnesses sign in order, one under the other? The witnesses sign from bottom to top.
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is answered by explaining how the witnesses actually sign, which removes the forgery worry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The questioner pictured signatures stacked one under another, which could keep growing along with the text. In fact, each signature runs upward from the back of the last line toward the first line, sideways to the writing. Any text added on the front would run past where the signatures begin and would be spotted as a forgery.

keyTerms.meaning: In their usual order; here, one under the other from the top
From bottom to top
They sign

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב ירמיה בר אבא, the witnesses' signatures run sideways to the text, from bottom to top. Because of this, the document cannot be extended without the change showing.

phrases.english: He said to him: Do you think
the witnesses sign in order?
phrases.notes: 'In order' here means stacked one under another, the way lines of text run.

phrases.english: The witnesses sign from bottom to top.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ מִי סָבְרַתְּ עֵדִים כְּסִדְרָן חֲתִימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the forgery challenge from Step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Corrects the questioner's picture of how witnesses sign.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The witnesses sign one under another, so their signatures could be extended to cover added text.
steps.terutzMaskana: The witnesses sign from bottom to top, sideways to the text, so added text would be noticed.

steps.title: What if he cuts off the last line along with the witness's first name?
steps.stepSummary: A new worry: someone could cut off a harmful last line, and the first word of the witness's name with it, and the leftover 'son of יעקב, witness' would still be valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry: maybe something harmful to the document's holder is written in the last line. He cuts off that last line, and the name 'ראובן' gets cut off with it. The document still looks valid, because 'son of יעקב, witness' is left, and we learned in a משנה that signing 'son of so-and-so, witness' is valid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the sideways signing method from Step 4. It shows a way someone could still cheat by cutting off the last line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witnesses' names run sideways, so the first word of a name ('ראובן') can sit right beside the last line of writing. If a cheater cuts off that line, 'ראובן' disappears with it. The rest, 'בן יעקב עד', is still a kosher signature according to a משנה, so nobody would notice anything wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us be worried that… (opens a concern)
Something harmful or damaging (here, to the holder of the document)
The last line of the document
He cuts off
As we learned in a משנה
Valid

phrases.english: But let us worry that perhaps something harmful happens to be
in the last line,
and he cuts off the last line
and cuts off 'Reuven' along with it,
phrases.notes: ראובן בן יעקב is just a sample witness name. 'ראובן' is the word sitting next to the last line.

phrases.english: and it becomes valid with 'son of Yaakov, witness';
as we learned: 'Son of so-and-so, witness' is valid!
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in גיטין 87b.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the sideways signing method that Step 4 gave as the answer
steps.kashyaTarget: The sideways signing method from Step 4
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Cutting the last line also removes the first word of the name, and the leftover partial signature is still valid by a משנה, so the cheating goes unnoticed.

steps.title: The name is split across two lines
steps.stepSummary: Answer: 'ראובן בן' is written on one line, and 'יעקב, witness' goes above it, so cutting the last line leaves only 'יעקב, witness'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where 'ראובן son of' is written on one line, and 'יעקב, witness' is written above it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the worry. The witness must split his signature so that 'ראובן בן' sits by the last line and 'יעקב עד' sits higher up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now, if the last line is cut, 'ראובן בן' goes away together, and only 'יעקב עד' is left. That is not 'son of so-and-so, witness', so the trick from Step 5 no longer works.

keyTerms.meaning: Where it is written
A line or row
Above it

phrases.english: Where 'Reuven son of' is written on one line,
and 'Yaakov, witness' is above it.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the document is only valid if the signature is written this way
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A signature written sideways can lose its first word and still be a valid 'son of so-and-so, witness'.
steps.terutzMaskana: The signature is split so that cutting the last line removes 'ראובן בן' together, leaving only 'יעקב עד'.

steps.title: But 'יעקב, witness' alone is also valid
steps.stepSummary: A follow-up worry: if he cuts off 'ראובן בן', the leftover 'יעקב, witness' is still a valid signature by a משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us worry: maybe he cuts off 'ראובן son of', and the document stays valid with 'יעקב, witness'. We learned in a משנה that signing 'so-and-so, witness' is valid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from Step 6. Even the split signature leaves something valid behind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same משנה also says that a witness who signs just his own name plus 'witness' is valid. So 'יעקב עד' reads like a complete signature of a man named יעקב, and the cutting would still go unnoticed.

keyTerms.meaning: It becomes valid
'So-and-so, witness' (a signature with just a first name)

phrases.aramaic: וְלִיחוֹשׁ דִּלְמָא גָּיֵיז לֵיהּ לִ״רְאוּבֵן בֶּן״,
phrases.english: But let us worry that perhaps he cuts off 'Reuven son of',
and it becomes valid with 'Yaakov, witness'
as we learned: 'So-and-so, witness' is valid!
phrases.notes: Same משנה in גיטין 87b as before. Now 'יעקב' just looks like the witness's own name.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיחוֹשׁ דִּלְמָא גָּיֵיז לֵיהּ לִ״רְאוּבֵן בֶּן״
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The leftover 'יעקב עד' still matches the valid form 'איש פלוני עד', so the cheating still works.

steps.title: The word 'witness' is not written
steps.stepSummary: Answer: in this kind of document the witnesses do not write the word עד, so a leftover 'יעקב' alone is not a valid signature.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where the word 'witness' is not written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final answer: the witnesses leave out the word עד entirely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the word עד, cutting the last line leaves just 'יעקב'. That fits neither valid form from the משנה, so it no longer counts as a signature. The missing piece would be noticed, and cutting off the last line can't secretly change the document.

keyTerms.meaning: Where it is not written
Witness (the word normally added after a signature)

steps.whatToRemember: For signatures on the back of the document, the name is split so 'ראובן בן' sits by the last line, and the word עד is left out. That way, cutting off the last line always ruins the signature and the cheating would be caught.
steps.confusionAlert: Normally writing עד is perfectly fine and even typical. Leaving it out here is a special requirement only for this signing method. It does not make עד a problem in ordinary documents.

phrases.english: Where 'witness' is not written.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case further: the word עד is left out
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The leftover 'יעקב עד' would be a valid 'so-and-so, witness'.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without עד, only 'יעקב' remains, which is not a valid signature, so any cutting would be noticed.

steps.title: A second answer: the witness did write 'witness', but we know his signature
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another answer to the forgery worry. Maybe the witness did write עד after his name, but we know for a fact what this person's signature looks like. The sentence continues in the next part.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you prefer, you can say: really, he did write the word 'witness.' But we are talking about a case where we know that this signature...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is starting a second, different answer to the worry from Step 7 (that a leftover 'יעקב, witness' could still count as a valid signature). This line is only the setup, and the rest of the answer comes in the next words of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said the witnesses leave out the word עד, so nothing valid is left after the cut. This new answer says that עד really was written. It solves the problem a different way, because we know something definite about this signature. The end of the sentence, on the next amud, explains how that blocks the forgery.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And if you wish, say...': introduces a second, alternative answer
'Really' or 'actually': keeps the original assumption and answers another way
We know
A person's handwritten signature

steps.confusionAlert: This does not take back Step 8. It is a separate answer that the גמרא gives as another option. Each answer works by itself.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
Actually, he did write 'witness,'
where we know about it that this signature...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the Step 7 worry, in place of Step 8's claim that עד is not written.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the witness's normal signature is already known.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the witness wrote עד, a leftover 'יעקב, witness' would look like a valid signature after the cut.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if עד was written, we know what this witness's real signature looks like. How that blocks the forgery is explained in the next part of the text.
